setup: Around 300 BCE the great Eurasian grassland is winding down at one end and waking up at the other. The Scythians — the Iranian-speaking horse nomads who ruled the western steppe for five centuries — are being squeezed into Crimea by their eastern cousins, the Sarmatians. Three thousand miles east, on the harshest stretch of the same grassland, a different nomadic power is taking shape on the Mongolian steppe, where winters hit minus 40 and the only nearby wealth sits behind a wall. To the south, China is changing fast: the Warring States are fighting toward unification, and in 221 BCE the Qin First Emperor finishes the job, then sends 300,000 troops north to push the nomads off the grass and connect the frontier walls into the first Great Wall. That wall is the problem. It cuts the nomads off from the iron, grain, and silk they cannot make themselves — and the people most threatened by it, a confederacy called the Xiongnu, are about to organize at a scale China has never faced.

bridge: Chapter 1 set the stage: a Mongolian steppe full of competing nomadic confederacies, a newly unified China walling off the frontier and cutting the nomads off from the goods they needed, and a chanyu named Touman who sent his eldest son Modu to the rival Yuezhi as a hostage and then attacked them, hoping they'd kill the boy for him. Modu survived. He stole a horse and rode home. And almost everything that defined the next six centuries of steppe history grew out of that one betrayal.
setup: This is the chapter where the Xiongnu stop being one confederacy among several and become the first true steppe empire. Modu seizes power in 209 BCE — by training his guard with whistling arrows until they would fire at anything he aimed at, including, finally, his own father. Then he turns that absolute loyalty outward: crushing the Donghu to the east, driving the Yuezhi west in a migration that will eventually birth the Kushan Empire, and sweeping up the smaller peoples until he rules from Manchuria to the Altai. What makes this more than a conquest story is the machine he builds to hold it: a dual-wing command, a decimal army that is also the entire government, an annual assembly under the sky god Tengri, and a chanyu who claims to be Son of Heaven — the exact title China's own emperor uses. The Scythians proved nomads could humiliate empires. Modu is about to prove they could build one.

bridge: Chapter 2 ended with Modu at the height of his power: an empire stretching from Manchuria to the Altai, a political system no steppe people had ever managed before, and a chanyu claiming to be Son of Heaven — equal to the emperor of China. Meanwhile China had been changing too. The Qin dynasty had collapsed into civil war the same year Modu murdered his father, and out of that war rose the Han dynasty under a former peasant rebel named Liu Bang. By 200 BCE the two strongest men in East Asia — the new Han emperor and the Xiongnu chanyu — were about to meet on a frozen mountain.
setup: Liu Bang, now Emperor Gaozu, has just won a four-century-lasting dynasty and figures the barbarians need teaching a lesson. He marches north with a huge army and rides straight into Modu's masterpiece of deception, getting his vanguard surrounded at Mount Baideng for seven freezing days until he buys his way out by bribing the chanyu's wife. The humiliation reshapes the relationship for sixty years. What replaces war is heqin — "peace and kinship" — a system in which the richest civilization on earth ships silk, grain, and imperial princesses to the steppe and formally treats a nomad chief as its equal. Chinese officials hate every line of it, but every calculation says it's cheaper to pay than to fight an enemy who out-rides them on his own ground. The strange twist: all that tribute silk gets traded westward and quietly finances the road that will one day reach Rome.

bridge: For sixty years after Baideng, the Han managed the Xiongnu rather than fought them: silk, grain, and princesses flowed north under the heqin treaties, the Great Wall held as the border, and Chinese officials swallowed insult after insult because the army couldn't beat the nomads on the open steppe. That tribute was buying time, not safety — Xiongnu raids never fully stopped, and one in 166 BCE came within sight of the capital. A generation of officials had been grinding their teeth over the shame of it. In 141 BCE a teenager came to the throne who agreed with them.
setup: Emperor Wu — the name means "Martial" — spends a 54-year reign trying to break the Xiongnu for good, and it becomes the most aggressive military era in Chinese history before modern times. He sends a courtier named Zhang Qian west to recruit the exiled Yuezhi against the Xiongnu; the mission fails completely but brings back the first detailed Chinese knowledge of Central Asia, accidentally opening the Silk Road. At home he abandons heqin and unleashes a new kind of Chinese army — retrained cavalry under a servant's son, Wei Qing, and his prodigy nephew Huo Qubing, who seizes the Hexi Corridor as a barely-twenty-year-old and dies at 24. The campaigns drive the chanyu north of the Gobi and overturn the military balance of the steppe. But they also bankrupt the treasury, and when one general's defeat goes badly, the emperor's rage falls on the historian who dared defend him.

bridge: Emperor Wu's wars, from Chapter 4, badly wounded the Xiongnu — driving the chanyu north of the Gobi, opening the Hexi Corridor, and cutting the confederacy off from its richest trade routes. But the Xiongnu were not destroyed by Chinese armies. They still held the Mongolian heartland, still had the cavalry to raid, still ran Modu's political machine. What a century of war had stripped away was the one thing that machine depended on: unity. The empire's real killer would turn out to be its own succession.
setup: Around 60 BCE the system breaks. The chanyu title had always passed messily — sometimes son to son, sometimes brother to brother — and now as many as five rival claimants fight for it at once, splitting the confederacy down the middle. Two chanyus emerge, and each looks a different way for help: Huhanye turns south and does the unthinkable, traveling to the Han court to bow before the Chinese emperor in exchange for grain and protection, while his rival Zhizhi heads west and gets hunted down. The empire that once trapped a Chinese emperor on a mountain is now its client. From here the story splits for good — Southern Xiongnu settling as China's frontier guards, Northern Xiongnu clinging to independence and slowly being ground down, until in 93 CE the northerners are driven beyond the Altai and simply vanish from the records. Where they went is the question the next chapter has to face.

bridge: Chapter 5 ended on a vanishing. After a century of civil war and Chinese pressure, the Xiongnu split in two — the Southern Xiongnu settling as China's frontier guards, the Northern Xiongnu clinging to independence on the steppe. Then in 89 CE a combined Han and Southern Xiongnu force shattered the northerners, and by 93 CE their remnants were driven beyond the Altai Mountains and simply stopped appearing in Chinese records. They disappeared into the grassland heading west. Nearly three centuries later, a terrifying horse-warrior people called the Huns appeared at the other end of the steppe, north of the Black Sea.
setup: This chapter sits on top of one of history's great unsolved puzzles, and it has to be honest about it: are the Huns the Xiongnu? The evidence cuts both ways — a possibly-shared name, the right direction of travel, identical mounted-archery tactics, intermediate peoples in Central Asian records, similar bronze cauldrons, and even some East Asian DNA in Hunnic-era graves — but also a 300-year gap long enough to transform any people, almost no linguistic evidence, and the fact that both groups were multiethnic confederations rather than single peoples. Scholars have argued it for over a century without resolution. What is not in doubt is the destruction. Around 370 CE the Huns crush the Alans, destroy the Ostrogothic kingdom, and so terrify the Visigoths that they flee across the Danube into the Roman Empire — where mistreatment turns them into rebels who kill an emperor at Adrianople in 378. The Huns hadn't yet fought Rome at all, and they'd already cracked it.

bridge: The Huns arrived in Europe around 370 CE (Chapter 6) and set off a chain reaction: crushing the Alans and Ostrogoths, driving the Visigoths into the Roman Empire, and triggering the death of an emperor at Adrianople — all before they'd fought Rome directly. Over the following decades they stopped roaming and settled onto the Hungarian plain, the one patch of Europe that looks and grazes like the Mongolian steppe. There a leader named Rua turned the loose raiding bands into a disciplined extortion machine and forced Constantinople to pay him in gold. When the machine passed to two of Rua’s nephews in 434.
setup: The nephews are Bleda and Attila, and within eleven years Attila will be the most feared man in the world. He rules jointly with his brother at first — then, around 445, murders him, a fratricide that echoes Modu's patricide six centuries earlier almost too neatly to be coincidence. Sole ruler now, Attila runs the Xiongnu playbook in a European theater: a small Hunnic elite commanding a vast multiethnic empire of Goths, Gepids, and others, extracting gold from Constantinople through escalating tribute treaties until the richest city on earth is paying him protection money. Then he turns the same method west — a manufactured marriage claim becomes a pretext to invade Gaul, where for the first time his army is stopped in open battle, and then Italy, where a pope, a plague, and a failing supply line do what armies couldn't. His empire is built entirely on his own terrifying authority, which raises the obvious question about what happens when that authority dies.

bridge: Chapter 7 left Attila at the peak of terror and then dead — in 453, on his wedding night, drowned in his own blood. For nineteen years he had extracted more gold from Rome than any foreign power in history, sacked dozens of cities, invaded Gaul and Italy, and built an empire from the Rhine to Central Asia. But it was built on one thing only: his personal authority, his network of alliances, his reputation for violence. When he died, the machine had nothing left to run on. And he left no clear rule for who came next — the same flaw that had cracked the Xiongnu six centuries before.
setup: This chapter is the collapse and the reckoning. Attila's sons immediately quarrel over the succession, and the subject peoples they'd been holding down take their chance: in 454 a Gepid-led coalition shatters the Hunnic army at Nedao, and within a single generation there is no Hunnic state, no Hunnic army, no Hunnic territory — the survivors melt into the Goths, Avars, Bulgars, and Slavs of Europe. The empire that terrified two Roman worlds for a generation evaporates in an afternoon. But the chapter's real work is the legacy: the Xiongnu shaped Chinese statecraft for two millennia and opened the Silk Road; the Huns triggered the migration of peoples that finished the Western Roman Empire; and beneath both runs the template Modu invented in 209 BCE, the one every steppe empire down to the Mongols would reuse. The Scythians were the first draft, the closing argument goes — the Xiongnu the revised edition, the Huns the European translation.
